They walk through two long nights, speaking little and sipping often, while the stars wheel overhead. Pebble grows slower with every hour, and Ysra worries that she is thirsty, but Teyo says that striders can go many days without water.
On the third evening Teyo stops and points at a small flock of birds flying low across the sky. Sandgrouse, he says, fly to water at dusk, so he turns to follow them.
Late that night the birds lead them to a long crack in a low cliff, so narrow that Pebble has to turn sideways. Inside, in the cool darkness, lies a hidden rock pool, black and still as a mirror.

The old woman, Mother Sabe, keeps the pool, and she hands them each a full cup before they have said a word. When Ysra reaches for her coins, Sabe laughs and says that water is never sold at her pool.

Sabe tells them that her pool has never been so low in all her years, and that it has been falling since the spring. Heavy carts have rolled east along the old road for months, she says, and the guards turn back anyone who asks where they are going.

After a full day of rest, Ysra spreads Orla's map on the cave floor, and Sabe adds a mark in charcoal. That is the Stone Gate, she says, where the carts go, and the guards will not let anyone near it.
At dusk Ysra and Teyo thank Sabe and lead Pebble out through the narrow crack, with all the skins full. Sabe gives Ysra a handful of dates and tells her to keep her eyes open and her water close.
For two nights they cross a huge, flat plain of white salt, as hard and bright as a polished table. Teyo says that long ago this was the floor of a real sea, and Ysra finds a tiny shell in the crust.
At dawn, at the edge of the salt, a tall pillar of grey stone rises out of the sand, half buried. It is the first sign of the Channelwrights that Ysra has ever seen with her own eyes.

The carvings show wavy lines for water, rows of numbers and a long arrow pointing east. Ysra reads the numbers with her fingertips and finds that they are counted in hands, exactly like the marks on the well rope.
Ysra unrolls Orla's map beside the pillar, and the same small signs are drawn along the silver thread. Teyo kneels in the sand and says that the river is flowing somewhere far beneath their feet.
By mid-morning Teyo lies asleep in the pillar's narrow shade, but Ysra cannot rest. On the horizon, a wide blue lake has appeared, shining and trembling, with a line of green trees along its edge.
Ysra runs across the sand towards the shining water, her mouth open in a laugh. Teyo, who has woken in an instant, sprints after her and catches her arm before she has gone a hundred steps.

Teyo turns her round gently and explains that the ground is so hot that it heats a thin layer of air above it. Light from the sky bends in that hot air, so a piece of blue sky seems to lie on the sand like water.
Ysra sits down in the sand, red with shame, and says that she should have known better. Teyo laughs and says that everybody runs towards the false lake once, and that he ran twice.
At dusk they set out again, following the pillar's arrow, and Ysra sees a long black line along the eastern horizon. It is the cliffs, Teyo says, and somewhere in them is the gate.

For two nights they walk towards the black line, which grows taller every hour until it is a wall of rock against the stars. Near its foot the old cart tracks appear again, joining from the west like streams running into a river.

At dawn they hide in a dry gully, and Pebble lies down in the shade of an overhanging rock. From beyond the ridge comes a strange chorus of sounds: hammering, the creak of winches and the barking of orders.
At dusk Ysra and Teyo crawl up a dune and look over its crest. Below them, in the foot of the cliff, stands a vast stone gate, carved with waves and crossed by new iron bars.

In front of the gate stands a small camp of tents, huts and stables, with a tall flagpole flying the blue banner of the Well-Guild. Guards in blue coats patrol between them, and heavy locks hang on the iron bars.
Teyo takes a small brass spyglass from his robe, the only thing of value that he owns, and lets Ysra look first. The circle of glass jumps and trembles, and then, all at once, the camp springs close.

Through the glass Ysra counts barrels, hundreds of them, stacked in rows beside a long pond lined with clay. Men bend over the handles of winches, lifting water from a small channel in the cliff and pouring it into the pond.
All through the evening Ysra watches and counts, and slowly a pattern appears. The guards change places twice a night, and between the changes only two men watch the north side of the camp.

At first light Ysra looks again, sweeping the glass slowly along the line of huts. Outside the smallest one, a strider is tied, with a white patch on its nose that she has known since she was a child.
A moment later a guard opens the hut's door and pushes a figure out into the light. It is a thin, grey, tired man with a ragged beard, and it is Dorin Vell, alive.
Ysra presses her fist against her mouth to stop herself from crying out. Teyo lays a steady hand on her shoulder and says quietly that now, at least, they know exactly where to go.
All day in the gully, Ysra and Teyo plan what to do. Ysra draws the camp in the sand, with every hut and every guard, and Teyo studies it as if it were a poem.

Teyo explains that in cliff country a whistle bounces from rock to rock, so that nobody can tell where it began. If he stands on a far dune when the guards change, he says, he can lead every man in the camp the wrong way.
Ysra will do the dangerous part: creep into the camp, find the hut and free her father while the guards chase the sound. Pebble will wait in the gully, hidden, ready to carry them all away.

Late that night, after the guards have changed, Ysra and Teyo creep down through the broken ground on the north side of the camp. Teyo squeezes her hand once, whispers good luck and slips away into the darkness towards the far dune.

A long, wild whistle rises from a far dune, then another from the cliffs, then a third from somewhere behind the camp. Shouting guards come running out of their tents, snatching up spears and lanterns and chasing the sound.

One guard, running late, stops only an arm's length from Ysra's hiding place and swings his lantern round. She holds her breath and counts, one, two, three, until he curses and runs on after the others.
Ysra darts from shadow to shadow until she reaches the smallest hut. A heavy wooden bar lies across its door, and she lifts it little by little, with her whole weight, without a sound.
Inside the dark storeroom, Dorin is sitting on a pile of sacks, and he looks up as the door opens. When he sees who it is, he cannot speak, and he simply takes Ysra's face in both his hands.

In whispers, Dorin tells her that the men in grey cloaks brought him here, because he had found out what the Guild was doing. They have kept him alive, he says, because Stane wants his name on a new law about water.

Dorin says that Stane has closed the Stone Gate on purpose, to dry up the Deep Well and to store the river's water for himself. Once the city is desperate, the Guildmaster will sell the water back to it at any price he likes.
Dorin is so weak that Ysra has to hold him up, and every step across the sand is slow. They are halfway to the northern shadows when the whistling suddenly stops.
A horn blares from the south, and torches blaze up all around the camp. Over the hard ground glides a long, flat skiff with a tall white sail, and it is full of armed men.

From the first skiff steps Rhodric Stane in a cloak of pale silk, as calm as if he had just come out of his garden. He walks slowly towards them, smiling, and says that this is a very pleasant surprise.
Stane knows exactly who she is: the clever girl who counts everything. He offers her a house with a fountain and a place in the Guild if she will go home and say nothing.

Ysra does what she always does when she is frightened: she counts the guards, the torches and the steps to the dark. Then she tells Stane that water is a promise, and that a promise cannot be bought, however fine the house.
The smile slides off Stane's face like oil off a hot stone, and his voice turns cold. He tells his guards to seize the two of them and to find the whistler on the dune.

Then a piercing whistle shrieks right behind the guards, so close that every man jumps and spins round. In that single moment, a figure in a blue robe appears out of the dark, seizes Ysra's hand and shouts, “This way!”
The three of them race along a narrow path at the foot of the cliff, with Dorin leaning heavily on his daughter. Behind them the guards shout and the torches bob like angry fireflies.

Ysra remembers a small sign on Orla's map, a door drawn beside the gate, and leads them to a fallen rock at its foot. Behind the rock, almost hidden, is a low door cut into the cliff, and Teyo drags it open with a screech.

They tumble into the darkness, and Teyo drags the door shut and wedges it with a stone. Then he strikes a spark, lights a small torch and holds it high, and a long stone tunnel springs out of the darkness.

In the torchlight the walls of the tunnel glow with paintings, blue and gold and white, still as bright as the day they were made. Ysra, breathless, turns slowly round and round, and for a moment even the hammering seems far away.

The first great painting is a map in which rivers spread across the wall like the veins in a leaf. A single silver line, wider than the rest, runs through the middle of the picture, and it divides into branches as it goes.

The next paintings tell the river's story: rain on the mountains, water sinking into sand, and a great gate with a wheel beside it. Beyond the gate, channels carry the water to a city where people are drinking and smiling.

Dorin whispers that the Channelwrights were teachers as well as builders, and that they painted these walls for the people who would come after them. Everything we need to know is here, he says, if we are clever enough to read it.

Beside the picture of the wheel, Ysra finds a table of numbers, with turns on one side and hands of water on the other. Her eyes fly down the columns, and every number goes into her memory, where she keeps things safe.

A tremendous crash echoes down the tunnel as the bronze door finally gives way, and the torches of the guards flicker at the far end. Teyo seizes Dorin's arm, and the three of them hurry deeper into the cliff.

The tunnel ends in a round chamber, and in the middle of it stands a huge iron wheel, taller than two men. Heavy chains are wound round its spokes like snakes around a branch, and a great lock hangs from them.
Teyo and Ysra pull on the chains, but the links are as thick as a man's wrist, and the lock does not even rattle. Without the Guildmaster's key, Dorin says wearily, nobody will ever turn this wheel.

Ysra shuts her eyes and walks back through the painted tunnel in her mind, until she reaches the picture of the wheel. In its corner, almost too small to notice, is a second wheel, set low in a wall, with an arrow pointing to a channel.

Dorin laughs for the first time in weeks, because it is exactly like the Channelwrights to build two ways into everything. Teyo is already on his knees at the foot of the wall, running his fingers over the stones and listening for a hollow sound.
Teyo taps every stone near the floor while Ysra, who sees the painting in her mind, tells him where to go. At the eleventh stone, the sound changes from a dull thud to a hollow knock.
Teyo works the stone loose, and it slides out of the wall with a grinding noise. Behind it, in a deep recess, is a wheel of green bronze, hardly higher than a kneeling man.
Down the tunnel a voice booms, “Stop, in the Guildmaster's name!” It is Captain Harl, the commander of the camp, and behind him thirty torches turn the painted walls red.

The wheel is stiff with age, and at first it will not move, however hard the three of them pull on the spokes. Teyo jams his staff between the spokes to make a lever, and all three of them throw their weight on it.

With a groan that seems to come from the heart of the rock, the wheel gives way and turns a quarter of a circle. Far below the floor, something heavy shifts, and a deep rumble starts to travel through the stone.

As the turns pile up, the rumble becomes a roar, and behind the wall the sound of rushing water grows louder every moment. A fine spray of cold mist begins to leak out through the cracks in the stones.
On the ninth turn, a section of the wall swings aside like a door, and the Silver Vein pours into the chamber. Teyo grabs Dorin, and the three of them scramble up onto a high stone ledge.

The water races across the floor and foams into the tunnel, where the guards turn and run for the door, shouting. One by one the torches go out, Teyo's last of all, and the chamber falls into complete darkness.

In the black, roaring dark, the three of them cling to the ledge and to one another while spray soaks their clothes. Ysra counts her heartbeats, one hundred, two hundred, three, and holds tight to her father's hand.

After a long time the roar settles into a steady rushing sound, and the water finds its way out through a low arch. High above them, a thin grey light appears at the top of a staircase, and Teyo says that it must be the dawn.
They climb out onto a ledge high on the cliff, into the pink light of morning. Far below, a wide silver river pours out of an arch beside the Stone Gate and runs straight across the desert, shining.
The wall of Stane's clay pond cracks under the rush, and all the water he has stolen pours back into the river. Dozens of toppled barrels bob and spin away in the current like toys in a bath.

In the camp below, the guards and the winch-men stand quite still, staring at the river as if they have never seen water before. Some of them kneel down, cup their hands and drink, and nobody tells them to stop.

Stane, who has spent the night hunting for the runaways, strides down to the water with muddy robes and a face white with rage. He screams at the winch-men to go into the tunnel, find whatever the intruders opened and close it again at once.

One of the winch-men, a broad grey-bearded man named Tobin, lays down his crank handle and says, “No, sir, we will not.” He says that his own children are thirsty too, and that he is tired of guarding water for a man who will not share it.

Stane threatens to cut their wages and to jail them, but the men only look at him and say nothing. Even Captain Harl, who has come out of the tunnel dripping, sits down on a barrel and folds his arms.

Alone now, Stane backs away, still shouting, and then he turns and runs up the slope to his skiff, followed by two guards. Within minutes the white sail is racing away to the west, towards Oshenar, and Ysra understands at once what he means to do.

Captain Harl walks over to Ysra and hands her a thick, stained book that records every barrel the camp has ever filled. He says gruffly that she is good with numbers, so she will know what to do with it.
Teyo runs to the gully and comes back leading Pebble, who is delighted to see them. Dorin's own strider is led out of the stables, and soon the little party is riding west beside the new river.

That night they camp on the bank of the new river, and Ysra kneels at the water's edge and washes her dusty face. The river whispers and chuckles beside her, and for the first time in weeks she falls asleep without counting anything.
As they ride west along the channel, the dry banks begin to turn green. Seeds that have slept in the sand for years are waking up, Teyo says, and tiny shoots push up where the water soaks in.

A band of Sandwrights rides out of the desert to see the new river, led by a tiny old woman with eyes like black stones. She is Amma Zeri, Teyo's grandmother, and she says that the book of the desert has a new page.

On the fifth day a Guild skiff glides up with Tobin and six other winch-men, lent by Captain Harl. They carry Stane's steel padlock, still stamped with his silver seal, and they have come to tell the truth in Oshenar, whatever it costs.

By firelight, Ysra reads Captain Harl's tally book from the first page to the last. When she compares its totals with the fall of the Deep Well, the numbers match almost exactly, and she knows that she has proof.

On the seventh day they climb a dune and see Oshenar, small and golden in the distance. The stone channel runs straight towards it, and a crowd is gathering on the east wall to watch the silver ribbon creep nearer.

Hooded and dusty, Ysra, Dorin and Teyo slip through the Sunrise Gate with the cheering crowd, and nobody looks at them twice. At the bakery next to the shop, Maro opens the door, drops his rolling pin and bursts into tears.

That night Pell sneaks in through the bakery's back door and throws herself into Ysra's arms, and Granny Orla follows with a lantern, weeping happily. The old woman touches the worn map in Ysra's pack and says that it was always meant to be walked, not kept in a box.

Five days later, the whole city crowds into the Well-House square, because the Rope Keeper has sent word that the Deep Well is rising. When he hauls up his rope, its wet part is a full hand longer than before, and a great cheer goes up.
Then Rhodric Stane climbs the platform in a fresh blue robe and raises his arms. It was the Guild, he cries, and his own brave engineers who opened the Silver Vein and saved Oshenar from the desert.

In the middle of the cheering, Ysra feels her father's hand tighten on hers, and she knows that she cannot stay silent. She pushes through the crowd to the foot of the platform and says, in a clear voice, “That is not true.”

Stane smiles sadly and tells the crowd that this poor girl has had a terrible shock, and that her grief has confused her. At his nod, two guards in blue coats step down from the platform and start to push towards Ysra.

Dorin and Teyo stand beside her, and from the crowd steps Tobin, the grey-bearded winch-man, holding up a great steel padlock. He says that he guarded the Stone Gate for months, and that this lock and its silver seal belong to the Guildmaster.

Ysra opens Captain Harl's tally book and reads out its figures, one barrel count after another, in her clear counting voice. They match the fall of the Deep Well, she says, and every page is signed by the Guild's own captain.
Stane shouts that the book is forged, the lock is a trick and these people are rebels paid by his enemies. But the crowd has stopped cheering, and the people look from him to Ysra with troubled eyes.

Elder Maris Thorne, the oldest member of the Well-Council, rises slowly from her seat beside the platform. She says that the Council will hear every side calmly in the great hall, and that nobody is to be arrested until then.

For two days the Council listens in the great hall to Tobin and the winch-men, to Dorin and Teyo, and to Ysra with her maps. They study the padlock, the tally book and the drawing she has made of the paintings in the tunnel.

At the end every member of the Council votes to take the Guildmaster's silver seal from Rhodric Stane and to judge him in open court. Stane, for the first time in his long slippery life, finds that he has nothing smooth left to say.

The Council's guards lead Stane out into the street, where the crowd goes silent as he passes, and then begins to cheer. At the back, Fennick Dray, the thin man in the grey coat, tries to slip out, but Maro and his big sons block the door.

That night, in the quiet hall, Elder Maris asks Ysra what the city should do now, since Stane's rule is broken. Ysra thinks of the line carved in the tunnel and of her father's cup, and she begins to speak.

Ysra proposes the Open Well Law, which has three rules, and she counts them off on her fingers. Every home gets a fair share, the well is measured in public, and the Sandwrights guard the Gate with the city.

At sunrise the Council votes to pass the Open Well Law, and Elder Maris reads it aloud from the platform where Stane once stood. A great cheer rises from the square, and it seems that the whole city is laughing and crying at once.

The Council asks that the Vell family's brass cup become the city's measure, and Dorin gently takes it from Ysra's hand. It is set on a white stone pillar in the square, and a smith promises Ysra a twin of it for her own pocket.

On the first morning of the Open Well Law, the queue stretches from the Well-House door right across the square. Little Pell is first in line, and the Rope Keeper fills her chipped clay cup to the brim by the measure of the brass cup.

Ysra holds out the finest dew-sail, the payment she promised, and Teyo takes it as gently as a sleeping bird. Then the Council asks the Sandwrights to be the keepers of the desert and the Gate, and Amma Zeri nods slowly.
Teyo accepts for his people, and Amma Zeri's camp will guard the Gate with the city's keepers. For himself, he says with a grin, he is still a walker, and he cannot promise to stand still.

As the weeks go by, Dorin grows strong again, and one morning he offers the shop to Ysra, saying that it is hers now. She says that she will be a merchant, as he was, and a keeper of the Stone Gate too, with honest ledgers for both.

Along the great stone channel, the people of Oshenar plant palm trees and gardens, and the dry plain begins to turn green. Dew-sails are hung over every roof in the city, and each morning the rooftops sparkle with drops.

A year later a terrible drought dries the plains and the far hills, and the rains fail for months. In the old days Oshenar would have been in danger, but now the Silver Vein runs steadily and the Open Well Law shares every drop.

Every morning Ysra reads the rope with the Rope Keeper and writes the number on a great board in the square. Little Pell, who is eight now, counts along with her out loud, and numbers feel friendly again.

At dawn Ysra stands on the roof again, filling her clay jars as the sun rises over a city that is green and awake. A long, low whistle comes on the wind, and Ysra pockets the small brass cup and goes down to meet her friend.

Every street ran inward like a spoke towards the round stone Well-House at the centre, where the first water-carriers already queued with their empty buckets. Beyond the outermost wall there was nothing except sky and sand, and the city huddled against that emptiness as if it were afraid of it.

Ysra had counted things for as long as she could remember, because numbers were the one part of a dry and uncertain world that always behaved themselves. She knew that there were fourteen stairs to the roof, twelve jars on the shelf and nine hundred and forty steps from her door to the well. Her father liked to say that she had been born with an abacus where other children kept a rattle.

Downstairs, her father Dorin was already throwing open the heavy wooden shutters of the family shop, humming a tune that had no beginning and no end. On a hook beside the door hung the old brass cup, polished by three generations of Vell hands until it shone like a small sun. Every customer who came through that door saw it first, and every one of them knew exactly what it meant.

The first customer was Maro the baker, who arrived every morning with flour on his eyebrows and asked for three cups for his ovens. Dorin filled the brass cup to the very brim, tilted it gently until the water shivered, and poured it out without losing a single drop. Ysra, watching from the stairs, had seen the same small ceremony thousands of times and had never once grown tired of it.

When Maro had gone, Ysra asked her father why he fussed so much over a single drop, since the customer would never notice it. Dorin only smiled, ran a thumb along the rim of the cup and said that water was a promise, and that a promise was worth nothing unless it stayed the same size for rich and poor alike. She wrote the sale in the ledger in her neat, upright hand, and for once she did not count anything at all, because she was thinking.

Pell, the seven-year-old from next door, appeared at the counter with her chipped clay cup held out in both hands, exactly as she did every morning. Ysra filled it for nothing, as she always did, while the little girl asked in a very serious voice why the desert had to be so enormous. Ysra, who had no answer, said that perhaps the world needed a great deal of room for all its secrets.

By noon the market square had filled with the chatter of spice sellers, the clink of copper scales and the flapping of striped awnings that kept off the worst of the sun. Above every stall hung the blue banner of the Well-Guild, a reminder, if anyone needed one, that most of the city's water passed through the Guild's hands before it reached anyone else's. Ysra threaded through the crowd with a basket on her arm, listening to the talk with half an ear.

Near the fruit stalls the whispers began, passing from one cupped hand to the next like a coin nobody wanted to be left holding: the Deep Well was falling. Ysra noticed that the queue outside the Well-House stretched past the dyer's shop, which was farther than she had ever seen it, and that no one standing in it was talking. She counted forty heads, then gave up, because the number no longer felt friendly.

At dusk Ysra followed her father down to the Well-House, where the old Rope Keeper held up his lantern so that they could see the long wet rope that hung into the dark. The knots tied along it measured the water in hands, and the last wet knot was three hands lower than it had been a month ago, which was a fall nobody in Oshenar had ever seen. Dorin said nothing on the walk home, and Ysra, who knew her father's silences as well as she knew her sums, felt a small cold fear begin to count itself in her chest.

The next morning a great bronze bell began to toll from the tower of the Guild Hall, and the shops of Oshenar emptied one after another into the square. Shopkeepers, water-carriers and weavers stood shoulder to shoulder in the heat, murmuring and craning their necks towards a high wooden platform draped in blue. Ysra and her father pressed through the crowd until they found a place beside a pillar, close enough to see and far enough to leave quickly.

Rhodric Stane, the Guildmaster of the Well-Guild, climbed the steps of the platform slowly, as a man does when he knows that every eye is upon him. His blue silk robes whispered around his ankles, silver rings glittered on every finger, and when he began to speak his voice was as smooth and warm as oil poured over a hot pan. Ysra, who disliked him at once and could not have said why, folded her arms and listened.

Stane told the crowd, with a grave face and a catch in his voice, that the Deep Well was failing and that the desert itself had turned against them. The Guild, he promised, would stand between Oshenar and disaster, as it had done for centuries, but every citizen would have to be brave and make sacrifices. He paused there, and the whole square waited, as quiet as a held breath.

Then, with the sorrowful air of a man performing a painful duty, he announced that from the following morning the price of every cup of water would be doubled. A gasp went through the square like wind through dry grass, and somewhere near the front a woman began to cry. Stane raised both hands for calm and explained, in his oily and reasonable voice, that scarcity must be paid for, and that this was the only fair way to make the water last.

Voices rose all over the square, some angry, some frightened and some simply bewildered, until a line of guards in blue coats stepped forward and rested their hands on their sword hilts. Stane smiled around at them all, waved one ringed hand as if brushing away a fly, and reminded everyone that the Guild could hardly be blamed for the weather. The crowd muttered and shuffled, but nobody dared to say aloud what half of them were thinking.

Back at the shop Dorin hung the brass cup on its hook, stood looking at it for a long moment, and said quietly that he would not double his price by so much as a copper. Ysra opened the ledger, dipped her pen and began to work out what that stubbornness would cost the family, column by column, down to the last coin. The answer was not a comfortable one, though she found that she did not mind it nearly as much as she had expected.

That night, by the light of a single lamp, Ysra went back over her figures, because something in them had begun to itch like a splinter. The well had fallen three hands in one month, yet the city had drunk no more than it always drank, and a well does not fall so fast by itself without a reason. She wrote the word why at the bottom of the page, underlined it twice, and then, because it frightened her, rubbed it out again.

The next day an old seamstress came into the shop, clutching a jug and a handful of copper, and confessed in a whisper that she could no longer afford the Guild's new price. Dorin did not hesitate; he filled her jug at the old price and told her that a promise did not change just because the weather did. Ysra wrote the sale in the ledger with a worried frown, for she could see exactly how many such sales the shop could survive.

At dusk Ysra carried two jars up through the winding lanes of the high district, where the richest families of Oshenar lived behind walls as tall as houses. At the end of a long wall she found a gap where a few stones had fallen out, and, being a girl who liked to know things, she put her eye to it. What she saw made her forget the weight of the jars entirely: a lush green garden of palm trees and splashing fountains, and above its gate the silver seal of the Guildmaster himself.

She stayed in the shadow of a doorway until the moon rose, and then, just as she had half expected, the garden gate swung open without a sound. Three heavy carts rolled out one behind the other, each stacked with barrels, and she could hear the water slopping inside them with every turn of the wheels. They crept away towards the eastern gate with their lanterns covered, like thieves who wanted nobody to count them.

Ysra ran all the way home, burst through the door with her hair coming loose, and poured out everything she had seen: the green garden, the silver seal, the barrels and the muffled lanterns. Dorin heard her to the end without once interrupting, which was not like him, and his face grew slowly older as she spoke. When she had finished he stood up, took a key from his belt and went to the old chest under the stairs.

From the chest Dorin lifted a map so old that its edges had worn soft as cloth, and he spread it carefully across the counter with the flat of his hand. It showed the great desert in faded yellow, the city of Oshenar as a tiny blue circle, and, running far beneath the sand, one thin line drawn in silver ink. Ysra had lived all her life in that city and had never once seen the line before.

This, Dorin explained, was the Silver Vein, a hidden river that crept slowly through the tiny gaps in deep sand and rock, filling them the way water fills a sponge. Rain had fallen on far mountains thousands of years ago, and the water had been travelling beneath the desert ever since, patiently and without any sound. It was this river, and nothing else, that had filled the Deep Well for as long as Oshenar had stood.

Long ago, said Dorin, the Channelwrights had been the engineers who dug stone channels to guide the Vein towards the city and who built a vast gate in the eastern cliffs to govern the flow. His own grandfather had told him stories about that Stone Gate, though no one living had ever claimed to have seen it, and most people thought it a legend for children. Dorin had always half believed those stories, and as he looked at the map in the lamplight, he believed them completely.

If anyone had blocked or turned the Vein, Dorin said, the Deep Well would keep falling until it was nothing but a dry black hole in the middle of the city. The only way to learn the truth was to go and look for himself, starting at the Cold Springs in the north, by the old road that wound east beneath the cliffs where the gate was said to stand. He spoke calmly, but Ysra, who noticed everything about him, saw that his hands were not quite steady, and the sight frightened her more than the map.

Ysra said at once that she would come too, and she said it three times in three different tones of voice, as if one of them might eventually work. Dorin shook his head each time, kindly but without giving an inch, and explained that someone had to keep the shop open, and that nobody was better with a ledger than his daughter. She argued until the lamp burned low, and lost, and went to bed at last, furious with him and prouder of him than she had ever been.

Over the next two days Dorin gathered his small caravan with great care: two drivers, one of them a cheerful, sunburnt man called Bastian, four long-legged striders and enough water skins to last a fortnight. Ysra counted every skin twice, then a third time out of pure nervousness, and each time the total came out the same, which was no comfort whatever. The city, meanwhile, grew quieter and sourer with every passing hour, as the Guild's new price began to bite.

At the Sunrise Gate, in the grey light before the sun, Dorin hugged his daughter hard and pressed the brass cup into her hands, saying that the shop and the promise were hers until he returned. If he was not back in ten days, he told her sternly, she must on no account come after him, for the desert was no place for a girl with nothing but a head full of numbers. Ysra nodded and promised that she would stay, and at that moment she meant every word of it, though the desert was already tugging gently at her thoughts.

The caravan filed out through the gate one beast at a time, the tall striders swaying like boats on a sea of light, with the rising sun turning their long shadows to gold across the road. Dorin turned once in his saddle and raised a hand, and Ysra raised the brass cup in answer, a foolish little salute that nobody could possibly see. She stood there, counting the beasts until she could no longer tell them apart, and then counting the seconds until even the dust had settled.

Ysra walked home with the brass cup tight in her fist, and for the first time in her life she unlocked the shop and pushed open the shutters by herself. The place seemed larger and quieter without her father's humming, and every shelf and jar looked as if it were waiting for him to come back and explain it. She hung the cup on its hook, drew a deep breath, took a piece of chalk and made one neat mark on the wall: day one.

Day after day Ysra opened the shop at sunrise, measured out the water with the brass cup and made another neat chalk mark on the wall, one more day closer to his return. Maro the baker, who had known her since she was in swaddling clothes, brought a warm loaf every morning and pretended he had baked too many. The neighbours were kind to her in a hundred small ways, and she was grateful, although she would have traded all their kindness for one glimpse of her father's tall figure in the street.

The Guild now charged the shop double for every barrel it drew from the Well-House, which meant that each sale ate a little hole in the family's savings. Ysra pored over the figures every evening and found that she could not make them balance, however she added them, and that a few weeks of such sales would empty the strongbox. Yet when she thought of doubling the price she saw her father's face, and the thought died, and she went on selling at the old price and eating a little less each day.

On the eighth day Pell came to the counter with her chipped cup and asked, in the blunt way of small children, whether Ysra's father had come back yet. Ysra said that he would be home very soon, and the word soon tasted strange in her mouth, like a coin that she was not sure was real. She filled the little cup to the brim and watched Pell carry it home with great care, step by step, as though it held the whole of the city's future.

On the tenth day, the day her father had promised to return, Ysra left the shop in Maro's hands and stood at the Sunrise Gate from noon until the sun went down. She watched every dust cloud on the horizon, and every one of them turned out to be only wind, or a stray goat, or her own hopeful imagination. When the lamps were lit the guards at the gate kindly told her to go home, and she went, counting her footsteps so that she would not cry.

Twelve days passed, then fifteen, and with each sunset the road beyond the gate remained stubbornly empty, until Ysra could hardly sleep for listening. The chalk marks on the shop wall had become a small forest of tally lines, and she could no longer look at them without feeling a tightness behind her ribs. In those long nights she began to understand that a number could be both perfectly correct and perfectly unbearable.

On the fifteenth evening a figure came limping along the road towards the Sunrise Gate, and Ysra, who stood there every sunset, knew from his walk that it was not her father. It was Bastian, the cheerful driver, but all the cheerfulness had been burned out of him, and he had no strider, no baggage and no hat against the sun. He sank down in the dust at her feet, and she knelt beside him and put the brass cup to his lips.

Between sips, Bastian told her that armed men had stopped the caravan on the eastern road, in a stony place where the old track ran close beside the cliffs. They had taken Dorin and the other driver and all the striders, he said, and then they had given him half a skin of water, told him to walk home and say nothing, and left him there. He wept as he said it, ashamed that he had not fought, though there had been twelve of them and only three of his own.

The next morning Ysra marched up the marble steps of the Guild Hall and demanded help in finding her father, and for a moment she felt rather brave. A polite clerk with an ink-stained thumb wrote her name in a thick book, nodded sympathetically and told her that accidents were common in the desert and that the Guild could promise nothing. As she walked out into the sunlight she noticed that the clerk had not asked a single question about where, or when, or who.

That afternoon a thin man in a grey coat leaned over the counter, resting his fingertips on the wood as if he were afraid it might be dirty, and smiled without any warmth at all. His name was Fennick Dray, he said, and for a sum he called generous he would take the shop, its stock and the brass cup off her hands, since a girl alone might be glad of the money. When Ysra refused, he did not argue; he only smiled, said that the price would be lower next week, and slipped out into the street as quietly as a draught under a door.

That evening a line of neighbours came to the shop door, hollow-eyed and quiet, and Ysra poured out her last full jar among them, a cupful for each, with Pell's cup filled to the top. When the shelves were bare and the door was shut, she sat on the floor among the empty jars with the brass cup in her lap and listened to the silence. By the time the lamp had burned down she had stopped asking who might find her father, and had begun asking when she could leave.

The next morning Ysra went from one caravan yard to the next, asking every master in Oshenar whether he would guide her east for any price she could name. They all shook their heads, some gently and some rudely, because the Glass Desert had swallowed too many travellers already and the Guild's guards had made the eastern road even less welcoming. By noon she had run out of yards, and when she sat down on the edge of a trough, she realised she had also nearly run out of hope.

On a dusty corner near the old tanners' quarter sat Granny Orla, who sold water by the ladle from a clay jar beside a tiny fountain that had almost stopped trickling. She had known Ysra since the girl was no taller than a bucket, and she took one look at that tired, stubborn face and put her ladle down without being asked. Orla was the oldest water-seller in Oshenar and had a reputation for remembering things that everyone else had decided to forget.

Orla listened to the whole story with her wrinkled hands folded on her knees, and when Ysra had finished she locked up her cart and led her into the cramped back room of her little house. There, to Ysra's surprise, the old woman knelt with a groan beside her bed and dragged out a flat wooden box tied with a faded red cord. Inside it, wrapped in a clean cloth, lay something that she handled as tenderly as a sleeping baby.

It was a map of the Silver Vein, drawn by hand in brown ink on thin leather, with the river marked by a silver thread and dozens of tiny signs that Ysra could not read. Orla's grandmother, she explained, had cooked for the last crews of the Channelwrights and had copied the map from a chest she was forbidden to open, and it had passed from mother to daughter ever since. Nobody had ever asked to see it, because nobody in Oshenar believed that the Vein could be followed.

Orla's warning was blunt and unhurried, as if she were reading out a list of prices to a customer. The Glass Desert, she said, had storms that threw sharp, glittering sand, lakes that were not lakes and dunes that wandered overnight, so that a lone girl would be lost before the second sunset. She took Ysra's chin in her dry fingers and said that the only safe way across was with someone who read the desert as other people read a letter.

The Sandwrights, Orla went on, were the people who lived in the desert and had learned its habits over many generations, and a small band of them was camped at the Old Cistern outside the east wall. They trusted nobody from the city, as a rule, and had good reason, but one young man among them was said to find his way by the wind alone and to whistle while he did it. Orla folded the map into Ysra's hands and told her that it would be a sin to leave it in a box any longer.

At noon, with the sun a white hammer on the roofs, Ysra slipped out of the Sunrise Gate and walked to the Old Cistern, where grey tents stood in the shade of a stone tank. Nobody stopped her and nobody asked her business, but a woman with a face like creased leather came out of the nearest tent and held out a cup of water before Ysra had said a single word. It was the first free cup she had been offered in weeks, and she drank it slowly, feeling it settle some of the knots inside her.

Beyond the tents, on a low rise, a young man in a long blue robe stood quite still, staring at a ribbon that fluttered from a pole as though it were telling him a story. Without turning round, he said that she walked like someone who was being chased by numbers, and then he did turn, and grinned, and introduced himself as Teyo. He was perhaps nineteen, brown as a walnut, with laughing eyes and a calm that made Ysra feel, for the first time in fifteen days, that she could stop holding her breath.

Ysra asked him straight out to guide her across the Glass Desert, and Teyo laughed and said that nobody sensible crossed it at this time of year, and that anyone who did was usually sorry. Then she unrolled Orla's map on the sand and held it down with four stones, and the laughter drained from his face as water drains from a cracked jar. He knelt, and traced the silver thread with one finger, and when he looked up his eyes were quite different.

They bargained for a long while, because Ysra offered every coin in the strongbox and Teyo refused them all, saying that copper was heavy and could not be drunk. At last he asked for something else: the finest dew-sail from her father's shop, a cloth that he had only ever seen once and had never forgotten, to be paid when they returned. Ysra, who would have promised him the whole shop, shook his hand on it, and Teyo said that they would leave in two nights, when the moon was thin and the Guild's guards were not looking.

In the old chest under the stairs Ysra found the dew-sail: a grey cloth as wide as a bed sheet and as light as a veil, woven so finely that it slipped through her fingers like smoke. Her father had bought it years ago from the Sandwrights and had kept it for some special day that never came. She held it against her cheek for a moment, breathed in the faint smell of dust and cedar, and folded it carefully into her pack.

Pebble, the family's old strider, lived in a stable at the edge of the city, because Dorin had judged her too gentle and too slow for the fast caravans. She was as tall as a doorway, with long pale legs, a patient lip and enormous brown eyes, and she studied Ysra for a long moment before lowering her great neck to be scratched. Ysra, who had learned to ride on her back at the age of nine, pressed her forehead against that warm, dusty neck and whispered that they had a long way to go.

Teyo came to the shop at dusk and laid a row of empty skins on the floor, explaining that the skins would pass the gate flat and be filled outside at the Old Cistern. Between the two of them, he said, a day in the desert would cost about two skins of water, even if they rested well, and the journey would take ten days or more. Ysra, who had been silently multiplying since the word ten, said that this made twenty skins at least, and Teyo stared at her as if she had pulled a rabbit out of her sleeve.

That night, while Teyo read out the old signs on the map, which meant wells, rock pools and warnings, Ysra filled a page with figures to work out how far their water would last. When she had finished she showed him the page, and Teyo read it twice, slowly, and then looked at her with a new and rather solemn respect. He said that in all his life he had met many people who could read a desert, but never one who could count it.

On the last evening Ysra gave the shop key to Maro and told him only that she was going to find her father, and that he must say nothing to anybody, above all to the Guild. The big baker, whose eyes were shining and whose floury hands were trembling, did not argue or ask a single question. He pressed a bag of flat bread into her arms, kissed the top of her head as he would have kissed his own daughter, and promised that the hook by the door would stay empty and waiting.

At midnight, under a moon as thin as a fingernail paring, Ysra and Teyo led Pebble through the silent streets, the folded skins lying flat across her back. Every footstep sounded enormous to Ysra, every shuttered window seemed to hold a watching eye, and the brass cup in her pocket knocked against her hip like a small and anxious heart. Teyo walked ahead with his hand on Pebble's bridle, whistling so quietly that it was more of a breath than a tune, and somehow it calmed her.

From the shadow of the last street, Ysra and Teyo watched a dozen guards in blue coats under hanging lanterns search every cart, every bundle and every traveller who tried to leave. Stane had ordered, a sleepy sergeant told the pedlar ahead of them, that nobody might carry water out of Oshenar and that the daughter of Dorin Vell, a girl with ink on her fingers, must not leave at all. Teyo glanced at her inky fingers, then at the empty skins folded flat across Pebble's back, and she saw him make a decision in the space of a breath.

Without a word Teyo lifted Ysra onto Pebble's back, laid her flat among the folded skins and buried her under a heap of blankets that smelled of smoke and goat. Then he took the bridle and strolled towards the lanterns, whistling softly, as calmly as a man going to market. Under the blankets Ysra counted her heartbeats, because she could think of nothing else to do, and reached two hundred and twelve before the first guard barked a question.

The guard demanded to know where a Sandwright thought he was going at such an hour, and Teyo replied, with a perfectly straight face, that his strider suffered from bad dreams and needed a long walk. The guard grunted and prodded the far end of the blankets with his spear, and Pebble, with the instincts of a true friend, stamped and let out a bellow that made the man leap backwards and swear. By the time he had finished swearing Teyo had pressed a handful of sticky dates into his palm, and the guard, who had not eaten since noon, waved them through.

Beyond the gate Teyo lifted the blankets, and Ysra sat up, shaking and laughing and gasping for air, with dust in her mouth and her whole body singing. At the Old Cistern two silent Sandwrights filled every skin from the great tank without asking for a coin, while Pebble drank for what seemed an hour. Then the two of them and Pebble walked out into the open dark, and the lights of Oshenar sank slowly behind them like a handful of embers dropped in a bowl of black water.

They walked all night under a sky so crowded with stars that Ysra could scarcely find the dark between them, with the sand whispering beneath Pebble's wide feet and the city already a rumour behind them. Teyo explained, in his easy way, that a sensible traveller walked while it was cool and rested while it was hot, because the sun drank more water from a walking body than any skin could carry. Ysra, who had always thought of the night as the time for sleeping, felt the whole world rearranging itself around her.

To Ysra's astonishment, the night turned bitterly cold, and within an hour she was shivering inside two blankets with her teeth chattering like dice in a cup. Teyo told her that with no clouds and very little damp in the air to hold the heat, the warmth of the day escaped into the sky almost as soon as the sun was gone. The same dry sky that cooked them at noon, he added cheerfully, would freeze them at midnight, and the only sensible answer was to be ready for both.

As the sky turned pink in the east, Teyo chose a spot in the lee of a large rock, drove two slender poles into the sand and stretched the blankets between them to make a low roof of shade. He unloaded Pebble, rubbed her legs, gave her a measured drink from a skin and let her kneel in the shade beside them. Ysra copied everything he did, a little clumsily, and discovered that being useful was an excellent cure for being afraid.

By noon the sand was too hot to touch, and the air above it shivered and wavered until the far dunes seemed to float. Teyo told Ysra to lie still, breathe through her nose and talk as little as she could, for every drop of sweat was water spent and every unnecessary word was a little more thirst. She obeyed drowsily, and counted the grains of light that fell through the weave of the blankets until the numbers melted into sleep.

On the second night, in the coldest hour before dawn, Teyo spread the dew-sail across a low frame of stones and sticks, tilting it gently so that one corner hung over a clay bowl. Ysra, who had spent half her life measuring water, could not see how an empty cloth in an empty desert would give her any, and she said so a little too sharply. Teyo only smiled and told her to go to sleep, and to be patient, and to be astonished in the morning.

At sunrise the dew-sail was beaded all over with tiny shining drops, like a spider's web after rain, and a thin bright thread of water was creeping from its lowest corner into the bowl. Ysra dipped one finger in and put it to her tongue, and the water was cold and clean and tasted faintly of dust and stone and morning. She laughed out loud, a cracked, delighted laugh she had not heard from herself in weeks, and Teyo, grinning, bowed as if he had performed a magic trick.

With a stick Teyo drew a picture in the sand and explained that even the driest air carries a little water that no eye can see, and that cold air can hold less of it than warm air can. The dew-sail cooled faster than the air around it during the clear night, so the invisible water gathered on its threads, exactly as it gathers on a cold jug brought into a warm room. It was never much, he admitted, only a few cups on a good morning, but a few cups could be the difference between a bad day and a worse one.

That evening, as they set out again, Teyo crouched beside wavy lines in the sand, as regular as the ribs of a fish, and told her that they were ripples and that the wind had written them. Each ripple, he said, had a long gentle slope facing the wind and a short steep slope on the sheltered side, so anyone who knew how to look could tell where the wind had been blowing. The wind in this country, he added, was the oldest and most honest map there was.

All that night Ysra walked a little ahead of Teyo, stopping again and again to crouch over the sand and trace the ripples with a fingertip, making a good many mistakes and learning from each of them. By the time the stars began to fade she could say with certainty which way the wind had blown the night before, and she found that the knowledge sat inside her like a small, hard, bright coin. Teyo, who had stopped correcting her an hour earlier, only whistled a long, low note of approval.

On the fourth night Teyo showed her the Lantern Star, a single bright point in the north that never seemed to move while every other star wheeled slowly around it through the hours. A traveller who could find it, he said, could never be completely lost, however many dunes might move and however many landmarks the storms might erase. Ysra counted her footsteps beneath it, a thousand, two thousand, three, and felt for the first time since her father left something that was almost peace.

On the fifth night Pebble stopped, flicked her ears and refused to take another step, and when Ysra looked ahead she saw why. Across the pale sand ran a pair of deep, dark furrows, ruled as straight as a line on a ledger, from one horizon to the other, with many hoofprints trampled between them. Someone had been using this road, and using it heavily, in a country that was supposed to be empty.

Ysra knelt and laid her hand flat in the nearest furrow, and then began to measure with her fingers and count with her lips, as she always did when she was frightened. The ruts were deep and wide and overlaid again and again, and from the number of separate wheel marks she reckoned that at least thirty heavy carts had rolled this way, probably over many weeks. Only very heavy loads, she said slowly, could press the sand down so far, and Teyo, for once, did not smile.

Teyo stood very still for a long time, looking east along the furrows with the look of a man trying to solve a riddle he did not like. In all the stories of his people, he said at last, carts carried water into the cities of the plain and never out into the desert, where there was nobody to drink it. Ysra felt the same cold unease that she had felt at the gap in Stane's garden wall, but this time it had a direction.

On closer study, Ysra saw that there were really two sets of tracks lying side by side, as a road has an outward lane and a homeward one, and that the two were not alike at all. The eastward furrows were deep and crushed, while the westward ones were scarcely more than scratches, and a girl who spent her days weighing cups of water had no trouble reading what that meant. The carts went out full, she said, and came back empty, and she knew exactly what kind of barrels had filled them.

They followed the tracks east, but at a careful distance, keeping low among the dunes and leaving no more mark of their own than Teyo could help, which was very little. Twice that night they saw the glow of a lantern far ahead, bobbing along the road like a wicked little star, and twice they lay flat on the cold sand until it had passed. Each time Ysra counted slowly to four hundred, because she had decided that a person who counted could not panic.

When the moon had set, Teyo built a tiny fire of dried roots at the bottom of a deep hollow, where the walls of sand hid every flicker from the road. They warmed their hands over it and ate Maro's flat bread and dates, and for a little while the desert felt almost friendly, full of the small crackle of the flames and Pebble's long, comfortable breathing. It was the first time since leaving Oshenar that Ysra had stopped listening for danger.

As the fire sank, Teyo told her the first law of the Sandwrights, which every child of his people learned before it could walk: water belongs to whoever needs it, and it is shared from the first day. A Sandwright who turned away a thirsty person, he said, ceased to be a Sandwright, and no tent would ever open to him again. It was the reason, he added, that his people had survived in a land where one selfish man could doom a whole camp.

Ysra asked what happened, among his people, to someone who kept water for himself while others went thirsty, and she thought of a green garden behind a high wall. Teyo considered for a while, poking the embers, and said that nobody would share a fire, a tent or a story with such a person ever again, which for a Sandwright was a worse sentence than any prison. In the desert, he said, nobody lived long alone, so being shut out of every circle was the harshest justice his people knew.

Teyo spoke then of his grandmother, Amma Zeri, who had taught him that the desert was a book written fresh every night, and that a person who could not read it was only a visitor. He had left the camp at fifteen, he said, because he would rather walk through the story than hear it told, and his people had sighed and let him go. His laugh, when it came, was a little rueful, as if he knew that he was explaining more than he meant to.

Ysra took out the brass cup and turned it in the firelight while she told Teyo about her father, and the promise of water, and the way that a measure could keep a city honest. He listened without a single joke, which she understood to be the highest courtesy he knew. Before she had finished he rose, tasted the dead air and said, in a voice she had not heard before, that the wind smelled of hot metal and that Pebble had been trying to tell them so.

Long before dawn a vast wall of copper-coloured cloud rose in the east and swallowed the stars one by one, and the air grew so still and heavy that it seemed to press on Ysra's ears. Teyo kicked sand over the embers, slung the packs onto Pebble's back in a few swift movements and said that a ridge of black rocks lay to the north and that they must reach it before the storm arrived. For the first time since she had met him he was not smiling, and that frightened her more than the sky did.

As they ran, Teyo shouted over his shoulder what he knew of glass storms, which were rare and terrible and had been named by his ancestors long ago. Lightning, he said, struck the baking sand and fused it into tiny beads of glass, and the great hot wind that followed picked those beads up and hurled them across the plain like handfuls of knives. No cloth could stop them and no face could bear them for long, and Ysra, who had never imagined a storm that could do such a thing, ran faster than she had ever run.

The ridge rose out of the dark like the back of a sleeping beast, and under an overhang Teyo found a hollow just big enough for all three of them, with Pebble folded down at the back. He tied blankets across the opening, wedged them with stones, wrapped a cloth around Pebble's eyes and told Ysra to cover her mouth and nose and keep her eyes shut whatever she heard. Then there was nothing to do but wait, and Ysra, who hated waiting, held the brass cup and listened to her own heartbeat.

The storm arrived with a long, rising roar, like a thousand carts rolling over a bridge of iron, and the dawn turned as black as midnight. Even with her eyes shut Ysra saw the lightning flicker red through her eyelids, and she heard the glassy grains hammer against the rocks and the blankets with a hard, hissing rattle that went on and on and on. The air in the hollow grew so hot and thick that every breath tasted of burnt sugar, and she pressed her sleeve over her face and thought, with perfect clarity, that she would very much like to go home.

After an hour of that terrible noise Pebble began to tremble from her knees to her ears and to tug wildly at her rope, and not even Teyo's strong arms could hold her still. In so small a space a frightened strider could hurt them all, and Teyo gripped Ysra's sleeve to say so, since no voice could be heard above the storm. Ysra crawled along the wall to the great creature's head, put her mouth beside one huge ear and began, very softly and very badly, to sing.

The song was an old counting rhyme that every child in Oshenar learned before it could read, about one cup and two jars, and it climbed through the numbers like a small determined animal up a hill. Beneath her hand the great creature's trembling slowly eased, as if the plain tune were a rope that she could hold on to, and Ysra kept singing, hoarse and breathless, round and round. Somewhere around the sixtieth verse Teyo, whom she could not see, joined in with a low voice that was slightly out of tune and entirely welcome.

It was many hours before the roaring thinned to a whisper and then to nothing, and the silence that followed was so enormous that Ysra's ears rang with it. Teyo pushed at the blankets, which had been buried by the drift, and a slide of warm, glittering sand poured into the hollow like water from a tipped jar. Together they dug themselves out on their hands and knees, with Pebble heaving herself upright behind them and shaking a small avalanche from her back.

Outside, the sky was a hard, washed blue, and the whole plain glittered with tiny beads of glass in green and gold and smoky grey, drifted in heaps against the rocks like spilled jewels. They chimed softly under Ysra's feet as she walked, a thin sweet sound like thousands of little bells, and she stooped to pick up a bead no bigger than a lentil and held it to the light. Teyo said that it had been plain sand an hour before the storm, and that his people called such beads the desert's tears.

But when Ysra turned to look for the tracks, there were no tracks, for the wind had buried them beneath a whole new range of dunes. Every landmark that Teyo had memorised, every low hill and hollow, had been buried or blown away, and the whole country lay like a bed that someone had stripped and remade. Teyo laughed and said that the desert had rearranged its furniture again, but she noticed that the laugh did not reach his eyes.

For a long hour Ysra stood silent among the glittering dunes, until she crouched and read the fresh ripples with her fingertips, as Teyo had taught her, and worked out that the storm had blown out of the east. Then she waited for darkness, and when the Lantern Star finally appeared, pale and steady above the new horizon, she knew exactly which way was north. Teyo, who had said nothing the whole time, bowed very low and told her that the Sandwrights would be honoured to call her one of their own.

When they checked the packs, Ysra found that a splinter of flying glass had slit one of the water skins from end to end, leaving the sand beneath it dark and damp where half a day's water had drained away. She stared at the stain for a long moment, then knelt and pressed her palm against it, as if she could push the water back in. Teyo said gently that the desert did not give refunds, and then, seeing her face, apologised for the joke.

Ysra counted what was left, then counted it again in case the first answer had been a mistake: eight full skins, which at their usual pace would last four days and not a single hour more. Teyo told her that the nearest rock pool he knew was at least three days away and might be five now that the landmarks had gone, so the arithmetic suddenly had a shape she did not like. They would have to make four days of water last for five or six, and they would have to start at once.

By the afternoon of the second day, Ysra's lips were cracked, her tongue felt like a strip of old leather and her head ached with a dull, steady beat. She sat in the thin shade with a skin in both hands, and every sensible thought she possessed was drowned by one enormous, ridiculous wish, which was to drink the whole thing down in one long swallow. Her fingers were already loosening the stopper when Teyo's hand closed gently over hers, warm and quite steady.

Teyo showed her how to take one small sip, hold it in her mouth until it had wet every corner and then let it slide down slowly, like a secret. Little sips taken often, he said, served the body better than one great gulp, and the real saving lay in resting, shade and silence, because a body that did not sweat did not need refilling. Ysra did as she was told and found, to her surprise, that a mouthful tasted like wealth.

They walked through two long nights, speaking hardly at all and sipping when Teyo said so, while the stars wheeled overhead and the glittering sand crunched underfoot. Pebble grew slower with every hour and Ysra offered her a cupful of her own ration, until Teyo gently pushed the cup away and explained that striders were built to endure thirst far longer than people. The kindest thing she could do for Pebble, he said, was to keep herself strong enough to lead her to water.

On the third evening Teyo stopped so suddenly that Ysra walked into his back, and pointed with a trembling finger at a small flock of birds flying low and fast across the darkening sky. Sandgrouse, he whispered, and they flew to water at dusk as surely as the Guild's clerks flew to their dinners, so if they followed the line the birds had drawn, they might be led to water. Ysra, her heart thumping, noticed a few tufts of grey-green lichen clinging to the rocks beside them, and for the first time in two days she dared to hope.

Following the line the birds had drawn, they walked for most of the night until, at the foot of a crumbling cliff, Teyo found a crack so narrow that Pebble had to be coaxed through it sideways. Inside, the passage opened into a small cool cave where a pool of black water lay perfectly still, and the smell of damp stone was the sweetest thing Ysra had ever breathed. At the pool's edge sat a tiny old woman with a lantern, who looked up at them as though they were late for supper.

The old woman, whose name was Mother Sabe, kept the pool for the Sandwrights and handed each of them a full cup before they had said a word, and then a second cup, and then a third. When Ysra, ashamed of gulping, fumbled for her coins, Sabe laughed until her small body shook and said that anyone who sold water at her pool would have to be a madman or a Guildmaster. By the law of the Sandwrights, she added, the pool belonged to whoever was thirsty, and tonight that was three of them, counting the animal.

Over a bowl of hot root tea, Sabe told them that her pool had never in her seventy years been so low, and that it had been falling since the spring, a finger's breadth each week. At about the same time, she said, the heavy carts had begun to roll east along the old road, and the guards who rode beside them turned back anyone who asked where they were going. She had counted the carts herself, with pebbles, because she was old and had little else to do, and the pebbles had long ago filled a jar.

After a full day of rest, with the skins brimming and Pebble round-bellied and glossy again, Ysra spread Orla's map across the cave floor and showed it to Sabe by lantern light. The old woman bent over it, tracing the silver thread with a crooked finger, and then took a stub of charcoal and drew a small firm cross in the east, where the thread met the cliffs. That was where the carts went, she said, to the place that the old stories called the Stone Gate, and she would not send a stray dog there if she could help it.

At dusk Ysra and Teyo thanked Mother Sabe, who would hear no word of thanks, and led Pebble out through the narrow crack with every skin full and heavy. The old woman pressed a twist of dried dates into Ysra's hand, kissed her on both cheeks and told her to keep her eyes open and her water close, because both were easily lost. She stood in the mouth of the crack with her lantern until the darkness swallowed them, a very small light on a very large plain.

For two nights they crossed a vast flat plain of white salt, as hard and bright as a polished table under the moon, where nothing grew and nothing moved and the stillness seemed to ring. Teyo told her that this was the bed of the old sea that gave the Dry Sea its name, drained away so long ago that not even his grandmother's grandmother had a story about it. Ysra, crouching to scrape at the crust, found a tiny perfect spiral shell as small as her fingernail, and she carried it for the rest of the journey in her pocket beside the brass cup.

At dawn, at the far edge of the salt, a tall pillar of grey stone rose out of the sand, half buried and leaning a little to one side like a tired traveller. It was carved from top to bottom with tiny, careful shapes, and when Ysra reached up and laid her palm against it the stone was already warm with the first sun. It was the first work of the Channelwrights she had ever touched, and she felt, absurdly, as if she were shaking hands with someone who had died a very long time ago.

The carvings showed wavy lines for water, columns of tiny numbers and, near the top, a long deep arrow pointing east, straight towards the cliffs. Ysra read the numbers with her fingertips, as a blind person reads a face, and realised with a jolt that they were counted in hands, exactly like the knots on the rope of the Deep Well. It meant that the Channelwrights had measured their river just as the people of Oshenar still measured theirs, and that they were not a legend at all.

Ysra unrolled Orla's map beside the pillar and held it up to the carvings, and the same small signs that were drawn along the silver thread were cut into the stone, every one of them. The pillar, then, was a marker, set up by the Channelwrights to show the line of the Vein, and the line ran right through the place where she was standing, a long way down. Teyo knelt, laid his palm on the sand as if he might feel something moving there, and said in a hushed voice that the river was flowing somewhere beneath their feet at that very moment.

By mid-morning Teyo lay asleep in the pillar's narrow shade, but Ysra, whose mind was too full of numbers to rest, sat up and looked east. There, low on the horizon, a wide blue lake had appeared, shining and trembling in the heat, with the dark shapes of palm trees leaning over its edge and a pale shore that seemed to beckon. It was the most beautiful thing she had ever seen, and she was on her feet before she had thought a single thought.

She ran across the sand towards the shining water, with her mouth open in a cracked laugh and every rule that Teyo had taught her scattered behind her like dropped coins. He woke at once, as Sandwrights do, and sprinted after her with his robe flying, and caught her by the arm before she had gone a hundred steps. The lake, Ysra noticed with dull surprise, was no nearer than it had been when she started, and it seemed to be retreating at exactly her own pace.

Teyo turned her round, held her by both shoulders and explained, very gently, that the sun had heated the ground until it warmed a thin layer of air lying right on top of it. Light from the sky bent as it passed through that hot layer, he said, so that a piece of blue sky seemed to lie on the sand ahead of them, shining like water. Nothing was there at all, and if she had followed it she would have spent her strength and her water and found only more sand.

Ysra sat down heavily in the sand, burning with shame, and said bitterly that someone who counted for a living ought to have known better than to chase a lake without checking the sums. Teyo laughed so kindly that she could not stay angry, and told her that everybody in the world ran towards a false lake once and that he, being slow to learn, had run towards two. Then he made her drink three careful sips, tied a wet cloth round her head and sent her back to the shade to sleep.

At dusk they set out again, following the arrow carved on the pillar, and as the last red light drained from the sky Ysra saw a long dark line on the eastern horizon, like a stroke of ink. The cliffs, Teyo said quietly, and somewhere in them, if the old stories and the old map were right, stood the gate that a race of vanished engineers had built to govern a river. Ysra put her hand in her pocket, closed her fingers around the brass cup and the little spiral shell, and walked towards it.

For two nights they walked towards the black line, and it grew taller every hour until it stood across the whole eastern sky, a wall of rock so high that it seemed to hold up the stars. Near its foot the cart tracks that the storm had buried appeared again, joining from the west and from the south like streams running into a river, until a dozen deep furrows lay side by side. Teyo made them turn off the road at once, and from then on they travelled in a wide curve through the roughest ground, where no cart could follow.

At dawn they hid in a dry gully, where Pebble knelt in the shade of an overhanging rock and Ysra lay on her stomach beside Teyo and listened. From beyond the next ridge came a strange chorus of sounds: the clang of hammers, the long creak of winches and, now and then, the sharp bark of a voice giving orders. Nothing in the whole empty desert had prepared her to hear a busy workplace in the middle of it.

At dusk Ysra and Teyo crawled up the side of a high dune and eased their heads over its crest, and there, below them, the Stone Gate rose from the foot of the cliff. It was an arch as tall as ten houses, cut from the living rock and carved from top to bottom with rolling waves, and it was so old and so grand that Ysra forgot to breathe. Across its mouth, ugly and bright against the ancient stone, someone had bolted a new lattice of iron bars as thick as a man's arm.

In front of the gate, spilling down the slope like a rash, stood a small camp of tents, huts, stables and storehouses, with a tall flagpole at its centre flying the blue banner of the Well-Guild. Guards in blue coats patrolled between the buildings in pairs, their spear-points winking in the last light, and fat padlocks as big as loaves of bread hung from the iron bars of the gate. Whatever the Guild was doing here, Ysra thought, it was not doing it by accident, and it did not want to be disturbed.

Teyo drew a small brass spyglass from the folds of his robe, the only object of any value that he owned, and after a moment's hesitation he let Ysra look first. At first she saw only a wild circle of sky and sand, jumping and trembling in her unpractised hand, and then, all at once, the whole camp sprang close, as clear as if she stood among the tents. She could see the stitching on a guard's coat and the dust on his boots, and she gripped the tube a little tighter.

Through the glass Ysra began to count, as she could never stop herself doing: more than two hundred barrels stacked in pyramids, a long clay-lined pond, and men bending over the handles of winches. The men were lifting water from a small channel cut into the cliff and pouring it into the pond, where it flashed like silver in the last light. It was the Silver Vein, she realised, trickling out through a tiny opening in the great gate, and Stane was keeping every drop of it for himself.

All through the evening and half the night Ysra lay on her stomach, watching and counting, and slowly, as numbers do when you give them enough patience, a pattern rose out of the confusion. The guards changed places twice a night, and between the changes only two men watched the northern side of the camp, where the ground was broken and a long shadow lay across the stores. She said nothing, but she drew a careful little map in the sand with her finger, and Teyo, looking over her shoulder, gave a long soundless whistle.

At first light, when the camp was just beginning to stir, Ysra swept the glass slowly along the line of huts, one by one, like a person looking for a lost word in a long page. Outside the smallest and meanest of them, among a cluster of tethered animals, stood a strider with a white patch on its nose, a patch she had known since she was a child. Her hands began to shake so badly that she had to rest the spyglass on a stone.

A moment later a guard pushed open the door of the hut and shoved a thin, grey, stooping figure out into the daylight, a man in a torn coat with a ragged beard. Ysra's breath caught in her throat, because even through the glass and across all that distance she would have known that stoop anywhere. It was her father, thinner and older and filthy with dust, but standing on his own two feet, and alive.

Ysra pressed her fist against her mouth to stop herself from crying out, and the tears ran freely down her dusty face and dripped off her chin onto the sand. Teyo laid a steady hand on her shoulder and said nothing at all for a long while, which was exactly the right thing to say. At last he murmured that after more than two weeks of walking they finally knew where to go, and that the rest was only a question of how.

All day in the gully, while the sun hammered on the rocks above them, Ysra and Teyo argued, whispered and planned. She drew the camp in the sand with a stick, every hut and storehouse and watch-post, while Teyo studied the drawing as if it were a poem in a language he was only beginning to understand. By the afternoon they had a plan, and it was so simple and so dangerous that neither of them could look at the other while they said it aloud.

Teyo explained the first part of the plan, which was entirely his own and which made him grin for the first time that day. In cliff country, he said, a whistle bounced from rock to rock until nobody could tell where it had begun, so that a clever man could make one note seem to come from three places at once. If he stood on a far dune when the guards changed, he promised, he could lead every man in the camp the wrong way for as long as Ysra needed.

Ysra's part was the more dangerous one: to creep into the sleeping camp, find the smallest hut and bring her father out while the guards ran after a sound that was not there. Pebble would wait in the gully with her bridle loose, ready to carry them away at a speed she had never been asked for in her life. It was a poor plan, Teyo said cheerfully, but it had the great merit of being the only one they had.

Late that night, when the guards had changed, Ysra and Teyo crept down through the broken ground on the northern side, bent double, stepping from shadow to shadow like cats on a wall. Where the slope levelled out, Teyo squeezed her hand once, so hard that it hurt, whispered a word of luck in the language of his people and melted away into the darkness towards the far dune. Ysra counted twenty slow breaths, because there was nothing else to do, and then began to crawl.

A long, wild whistle rose from a far dune, climbed to a shriek, broke into three pieces and came back from the cliffs, and then from somewhere behind the camp, and then from nowhere at all. The Guild's guards burst out of their tents in their shirtsleeves, snatching up spears and lanterns and shouting at one another, and half of them ran towards the dune and half towards the cliffs. Ysra, flat on her stomach behind a stack of barrels, almost laughed, and had to bite the corner of her sleeve.
