One guard, lagging behind with his boots half laced, stopped an arm's length from the barrels and swung his lantern slowly round, so that the yellow light slid across the toe of Ysra's boot. She did not breathe and she did not blink, and in her head, very small and very steady, she counted: one, two, three, four. At nine the guard muttered a curse about whistling devils and ran on after the others, and the dark closed over her once more.

She darted from shadow to shadow, from stack to stack and from tent to tent, until the smallest and meanest hut stood in front of her with a heavy wooden bar slotted across its door. The bar was far heavier than she had expected, and she had to put her shoulder beneath it and lift with her legs, little by little, an inch at a time, for fear that it would scrape. When at last it came free she lowered it gently to the sand and stood for a moment with her forehead against the rough wood, trembling from head to foot.

Inside the airless storeroom, among sacks and coils of rope, Dorin Vell was sitting with his back to the wall and his chin on his chest, and he lifted his head slowly as the door creaked open. For a long moment he did not seem to understand what he was seeing, and then his whole face changed, and he made a small broken sound that was not quite a word. He took his daughter's face in both his rough hands and held it, and looked at it, as a thirsty man looks at water.

In whispers, with his arm tight round her shoulders, Dorin told her that the men in grey cloaks had taken him on the eastern road and brought him here, because he had come too close to the Guild's secret. They had kept him alive, he said, only because Stane wanted the honest name of Dorin Vell on a new Law of Scarcity that would hand the city's water to the Guild for ever. He had refused to sign it for more than a month, he said, and he would refuse for a year.

Then Dorin told her the whole of it: that the Guildmaster had shut the Stone Gate on purpose, to dry up the Deep Well, and was storing the river's water here, behind the cliffs, for himself. When Oshenar was desperate enough, Stane planned to sell it back to the city, cup by cup, at any price he cared to name, and to rule it for ever afterwards as its only master. Ysra, who had spent her whole life believing that water was a promise, understood at last that to some people it was only a lever.

Dorin was so weak that Ysra had to take most of his weight on her own shoulder, and every step they took across the open sand felt as long as a mile. They were halfway to the northern shadows, with the shouting still ringing from the far side of the camp, when the whistling suddenly stopped. The silence that came after it was far worse than any noise, because it meant that either Teyo had been caught or the guards had worked out the trick.

A horn blared out from the south, so loud and so close that Dorin flinched, and all around the camp torches flared up one after another like a string of red beads. Over the hard ground, with a hiss like a snake, glided a long flat skiff on iron runners, driven by a tall white sail and crowded with armed men, and behind it came a second and a third. The fugitives dropped flat behind a heap of sacks, and Ysra, peering round the corner, felt every hope she had drain into the sand.

From the first skiff stepped Rhodric Stane in a long cloak of pale silk, with a silver-topped cane in one hand, as calm and clean as if he had just strolled out of his garden. A dozen guards spread out around him in a half-circle, and the torches threw such a bright light on the sand that there was nowhere left to hide. He walked slowly towards the sacks, smiling his smooth smile, and said in his oiliest voice that this was a very pleasant surprise.

Stane knew exactly who she was, he said, the clever Vell girl who could not pass a coin without counting it, and he was sure that a mind like hers must understand the arithmetic of the situation. He would give her a house with a fountain in its courtyard, a place in the Guild and enough gold to last three lifetimes, if she would simply go home and say nothing. Water, he told her softly, was only a number, and a clever girl could see on which side of the number she preferred to stand.

Ysra did what she always did when she was frightened, and counted: twelve guards, eight torches, forty paces to the shadows, and one old man who could not run. Then, to her own surprise, she stood up straight and told him that he had the sum wrong, because water was not a number but a promise, and a promise could not be bought at any price. Her father, beside her, took her hand and squeezed it so tightly that she knew exactly what he thought of her answer.

The smile slid off Stane's face like oil off a hot stone, and what lay underneath was cold, thin and entirely without mercy. He told his guards, in a flat voice that carried across the sand, to seize the father and the daughter and to find the whistler on the dune. The guards stepped forward as one, spears lowered, and the circle of torchlight began to close.

Then a piercing whistle shrieked out right behind the guards, so close and so loud that every man jumped and spun round with his spear pointing the wrong way. In that single moment a figure in a blue robe leaped out of the darkness, seized Ysra's free hand and dragged her to her feet, and a voice that she knew shouted, “This way, and run!” Teyo's grin flashed in the torchlight, a little the worse for wear, and she had never been so glad to see anyone in her life.

The three of them raced along a narrow path at the foot of the cliff, Dorin leaning heavily on his daughter and Teyo running behind, while the guards' torches bobbed after them like angry fireflies. Shouts and the clatter of boots echoed off the rock, and a thrown stone cracked against the cliff just ahead of them. Dorin's breath rasped in his chest, but he kept going, and she realised that he was muttering the old counting rhyme of Oshenar to give his legs a rhythm.

Ysra suddenly remembered a tiny sign on Orla's map, a little arch drawn beside the great gate, which Teyo had read as a way in, and she gasped that it must be close. They found it at the foot of the cliff, behind a huge fallen boulder, a low door of green-black bronze, almost hidden by drifts of sand and trailing roots. Teyo and Ysra threw their weight against it together, and it swung open with a long, rusty shriek that seemed to the three of them loud enough to wake the dead.

They tumbled into total blackness, and Teyo wrenched the door shut behind them and jammed it with a lump of fallen rock, while on the other side the boots of the guards came pounding up to it and stopped. Fists and spear-butts began to hammer on the bronze, and the sound rolled down the passage ahead of them like thunder in a well. Then Teyo struck a spark, lit a small pitch torch from his pack and held it high, and a long, arched tunnel sprang out of the darkness, running away into the heart of the cliff.

In the flickering torchlight the walls and the curved ceiling of the tunnel glowed with paintings in deep blue, ochre, gold and milky white, still as fresh as if the artists had put down their brushes that morning. Dry air and darkness had kept them safe for thousands of years, and for a long still moment even the hammering of the guards seemed to belong to another world. Ysra turned slowly on the spot with her mouth open, like a child in a room full of toys.

The first great painting was a map, and on it the rivers of the world spread across the wall like the veins in a leaf, blue and fine and branching. Through the middle ran one broad silver line, which began among painted mountains and divided into smaller and smaller branches as it flowed towards a tiny blue circle that Ysra knew at once was Oshenar. She laid her finger on that circle, and it seemed to her that the whole painting was pointing at it.

The next paintings told the river's story as plainly as a picture book: rain falling on high mountains, water sinking into the thirsty sand, and a great arched gate in a cliff with a huge wheel beside it. Beyond the gate painted channels carried the water on across the desert to a city of blue roofs, where tiny figures were drinking, laughing, watering gardens and filling jars. Whoever had made these pictures had loved the people they showed, Ysra thought, and had wanted them never to forget how their water came.

Dorin leaned against the wall, gasping, and whispered that the Channelwrights had been teachers as well as builders, and that they had painted these walls for the people who would come after them. He had heard it said by his grandfather, he told her, and had thought it only a story, as he had thought of so many things in his life. Everything they needed to know, he added, was probably painted here somewhere, if they were clever enough to read it before the guards broke down the door.

Beside the picture of the wheel Ysra found something she understood better than any painting: a table of numbers, with turns of the wheel on one side and hands of water on the other, as neat as a ledger. Her eyes flew down the columns, and every figure went into her memory, where she had always kept her sums safe. Beneath the table ran one line of the old script, which Teyo read aloud, slowly, one symbol at a time: “What the river gives, give on.”

A tremendous crash rolled down the tunnel as the bronze door finally gave way, and far behind them a red glow of torches flared and began to bob along the painted walls. Teyo seized Dorin's arm, Ysra seized the other, and the three of them hurried deeper into the cliff, with the pictures of the Channelwrights flashing by on either side like a procession of ghosts. Ysra tried to keep the table of numbers in her head with every jolting step, repeating it silently like a prayer.

The tunnel ended in a round chamber with a roof like the inside of a bell, and in the middle of it, taking up almost the whole of the floor, stood a vast iron wheel, taller than two men. It was the wheel from the painting, the wheel that governed the Stone Gate, and a tangle of heavy chains had been wound through its spokes and round its axle like snakes round a branch. From the chains hung an enormous new padlock of polished steel, stamped with the silver seal of the Guildmaster.

Teyo and Ysra flung themselves at the chains and pulled until the veins stood out on their foreheads, but the links were as thick as a man's wrist, and the great lock did not so much as rattle. Teyo tried his knife on the steel, then a stone, then the pry-bar of his own shoulder, and gave up, panting, with a rueful smile. Without the Guildmaster's key, Dorin said wearily, nobody on earth would turn this wheel, and the guards' voices in the tunnel behind them were already growing louder.

While the others argued, Ysra shut her eyes and walked backwards through the painted tunnel in her mind, picture by picture, until she stood once more before the painting of the wheel. And there, in its lower corner, so small that she had missed it in the flickering light, was a second wheel, much smaller than the great one, set low in a wall beside a channel. She opened her eyes and said, in a voice that surprised even herself, that the Channelwrights had drawn two wheels.

Dorin stared at his daughter, and then, for the first time in weeks, he laughed, because it was exactly like the Channelwrights to build two ways into everything: one for the strong and one for the clever. Teyo was already on his knees at the foot of the wall with the torch in one hand, running his fingers across the stones and tapping each one with his knuckle, listening for a hollow sound. The voices of the guards were very near now, and the first of the torches had begun to throw wavering shadows on the floor.

Teyo tapped every stone along the foot of the wall while Ysra, who could still see the painting as clearly as if it hung before her, called out directions: lower, three hands from the corner. At the eleventh stone the sound changed from a dull thud to a hollow knock, like a knuckle on the door of an empty room. The three of them looked at one another, and nobody dared to say anything, in case saying it made it untrue.

Teyo wedged his fingers round the stone and worked it loose, and it slid out of the wall with a grinding noise that echoed round the chamber. Behind it, in a deep recess lined with dust, crouched a wheel of green bronze, hardly higher than a kneeling man, its spokes crusted with the pale salt of ages. It had not been touched, Ysra thought, since before her own city had a name, and yet when she brushed the dust away she found the bronze underneath as sound as the day it was cast.

Down the tunnel a voice boomed, “Stop where you are, in the Guildmaster's name, and nobody will be hurt!” It belonged to Captain Harl, the commander of the camp, a heavy, tired man with a grey moustache, and behind him thirty torches turned the painted walls from blue to red. He had come to the mouth of the chamber, thirty paces away, and his men were fanning out behind him with their spears levelled.

The wheel was stiff with the damp and the salt of thousands of years, and at first it would not move at all, however hard the three of them heaved on the spokes. Teyo jammed his long tent pole between two spokes to make a lever, and then Dorin, Ysra and he threw their whole weight on it, grunting and straining, while the shouts of the guards came closer. Ysra thought of the numbers in the table, of turns and hands and the long thirst of Oshenar, and put her shoulder to the pole with a strength she had not known she possessed.

With a groan that seemed to come from the heart of the rock, the wheel gave way and swung a quarter of a turn, and then another, easier and faster, as if it were glad to be remembered. Far below the floor something heavy shifted, and a deep rumble began to travel through the stone, up through the soles of their feet and into their teeth. Ysra, who had been counting every turn without meaning to, gasped that eight more would open the drain, exactly as the table said.

As the turns mounted, the rumble grew into a roar, and behind the wall the sound of rushing water swelled with every revolution until it seemed that a whole river was pressing its shoulder against the stone. A fine spray of cold mist began to leak out through the cracks, and the air in the chamber, which had been stale and dry for ages, filled all at once with the sharp, clean smell of rain. Dorin, wide-eyed, whispered that he had never smelled anything so beautiful in his life.

On the ninth turn there was a great shuddering crack, a section of the wall swung aside like a door, and the Silver Vein came pouring into the chamber in a glittering rush of white water. It was the colour of molten metal where the torchlight struck it, and it came with a roar that shook the dust from the ceiling. Teyo seized Dorin round the waist, Ysra seized Teyo's sleeve, and the three of them scrambled up onto a high stone ledge with the water snatching at their heels.

The water raced across the floor and foamed into the mouth of the tunnel, where Captain Harl's men, who had been about to charge, stopped, stared and then turned and ran for the broken door. Their shouting dwindled and was lost in the roar, and one by one their torches went out, until only Teyo's was left, burning on the ledge. Then a spray of cold water struck it, it hissed and died, and the chamber fell into a darkness so thick that Ysra could feel it on her skin.

In the black, roaring dark the three of them clung to the ledge and to one another, while spray soaked their clothes and the whole chamber trembled like the inside of a drum. Ysra counted her heartbeats, because it was the only thing left that was hers to count, and held on to her father's hand as she had not done since she was very small. Dorin's other arm was round her, and she felt his chest shake, and realised, with astonishment, that he was laughing.

After a long, long time the roar settled into a steady rushing, as the water found its way out through a low arch in the far wall and the flood sank to a swift stream about their ankles. High above them, at the top of a flight of steps beside the ledge, a thin grey light appeared, and Teyo, who judged the hour by the feel of the air, said that it must be dawn. They climbed towards it, one hand on the wall and one hand on each other, three small figures stepping out of the dark into the first light of a different world.

They climbed out through a crack onto a ledge high on the face of the cliff, blinking in the pink light of morning, and for a long moment nobody spoke. Far below, a wide silver river was pouring from an arch beside the Stone Gate and running straight as a ruler across the desert, carried along a great stone channel that nobody in living memory had seen full. The sunrise caught it, and it blazed from end to end like a road laid down in light.

Before their eyes the wall of Stane's clay pond cracked under the rush of the new river, and then it gave way, so that every drop of the water he had stolen came pouring back into the river. Dozens of toppled barrels bobbed and spun away in the current like toys in a bath, and the pond, which had taken months to fill, was an empty, muddy hollow within minutes. Ysra, watching from the ledge, felt something so large and so joyful rise in her chest that it was nearly a pain.

In the camp below, the guards and the winch-men had stopped whatever they were doing and stood quite still, staring at the river like men who had forgotten that water could move. The soaked and shaken men who had fled from the tunnel came stumbling out of the broken door, and some of them dropped to their knees at the water's edge, cupped their hands and drank. Nobody told them to stop, because nobody in that whole sunburnt crowd had enjoyed a proper drink in weeks.

Stane, who had spent the whole night hunting for the runaways, came striding down to the water's edge with mud on the hem of his pale robes and a face gone white and shiny with rage. He screamed at the winch-men to go back into the tunnel, find whatever the intruders had opened and close it again, and he screamed it three times, as if volume might do what authority could not. For the first time since Ysra had known him, the oil had gone out of his voice.

A broad, grey-bearded winch-man, whose name was Tobin, put down the crank he was holding and said, quite politely, “No, sir, we will not.” He had a wife and four children in Oshenar, he said, and for weeks he had been guarding water that they could not drink, and he was ashamed of himself, and he would not do it another hour. One by one the other men laid down their tools beside him, until there was a long row of hammers, ropes and crank handles lying in the sand, each one a small stubborn refusal.

Stane threatened to cut their wages, to throw them in prison and to ruin their families, and when that failed he offered them gold, handfuls of it, flung down on the sand at their feet. The men only looked at him, and at the coins, and at the river, and said nothing at all. Even Captain Harl, who had come out of the tunnel dripping, sat down on a barrel, folded his arms and remarked that his wife and daughters lived in Oshenar and that he cared about them more than his pay.

Alone at last, Stane backed away, still shouting, and then he turned and ran up the slope to his skiff, followed by the two guards who were too frightened of him to leave. Within minutes the white sail was racing away to the west, towards Oshenar, as fast as the wind could drive it, and Ysra understood at once what he meant to do. He would reach the city days before they could, and tell a story of his own about the river, in his own smooth voice, before anyone else had a chance to tell the truth.

Captain Harl walked slowly over to Ysra, still dripping, and held out a thick, stained book with a blue cover, the tally of every barrel that the camp had ever filled, in his own neat handwriting. He had been ordered to keep it, he said, and he had kept it honestly, because honest figures were the only thing in this wretched business that he was proud of. She would know, he added gruffly, what to do with it, and Ysra, taking it in both hands, found that she did.

Teyo ran back to the gully and returned in under an hour, leading Pebble, who greeted Ysra by pressing her whole enormous face into her chest and nearly knocking her over. Dorin's own strider, the one with the white patch on its nose, was led out of the camp stables by a grinning guard, and Dorin hid his face in its neck for a long time without saying anything. Captain Harl's men, who seemed to feel that they owed somebody something, filled every skin and loaded the packs themselves, and watched in silence as the little party rode off along the bank of the new river.

That night they camped on the bank of the new river, and Ysra knelt at the water's edge and washed the dust of the whole journey from her face, her hands and her hair. The water was so cold and so clean that it made her gasp, and she drank it by the handful, slowly, in the way that Teyo had taught her, though there was no longer any need. Then she lay down on the warm sand between her father and her friend, with the river whispering and chuckling beside her, and fell asleep without counting anything at all.

As they rode west along the great channel, the dry banks began, hour by hour, to turn green. Seeds that had slept in the sand for years, even for decades, Teyo explained, were waking at the first touch of moisture, and tiny shoots, pale and fierce, pushed up wherever the water soaked in. By the third day the river ran between two ribbons of living green, and Ysra, who had never seen a desert in bloom, thought it must be the most hopeful sight in the world.

On the fourth day a band of Sandwrights came riding out of the desert to see the new river, led by a tiny old woman with eyes like black stones and a face as lined as a dry riverbed. She was Amma Zeri, Teyo's grandmother, and she stood for a long time looking at the water before saying, in a voice as dry as dust, that the book of the desert had been given a new page. Then she turned and took her grandson's face in both her hands, and Teyo, who was afraid of nothing, looked suddenly very young.

On the fifth day one of the Guild's own skiffs came gliding up behind them, lent by Captain Harl, with Tobin and six other winch-men standing in the stern and waving. They had brought the great padlock from the wheel, still stamped with Stane's silver seal, and they had come, Tobin said, to tell the truth in Oshenar, because a man could not sleep who had guarded a lie. Dorin, riding with the colour slowly coming back into his cheeks, shook each of their hands in turn and said that the truth was never wasted.

By firelight Ysra read Captain Harl's tally book from the first page to the last, running her finger down every column as she had once run it down her father's ledger. She knew from the Rope Keeper's old tables how much water a hand of depth held in the Deep Well, and when she set the book's totals against the fall of the rope, the figures matched almost exactly. Stane had taken the river's water barrel by barrel, and the Guild's own honest clerk had written down every one.

On the seventh day they climbed a high dune and saw Oshenar, small and golden in the distance, its blue roofs shimmering in the heat like a heap of dropped coins. The stone channel ran straight towards it across the plain, and at its mouth, on the eastern wall, a vast crowd had gathered to watch the silver ribbon creeping nearer, mile by mile. Ysra could hear the distant roar of cheering carried on the wind, and her eyes filled with tears at the sheer size of what they had done.

Hooded and dusty, Ysra, Dorin and Teyo slipped in through the Sunrise Gate among the cheering crowd, and nobody looked at them twice, because everyone was looking at the water. At the baker's door next to the old shop, Ysra knocked three times, and Maro opened it, stared, dropped his rolling pin with a crash and burst into tears. He pulled all three of them inside, bolted the door, and said, over and over, that he had known it, that he had always known it.

That night Pell crept in through the bakery's back door and threw herself into Ysra's arms so hard that they both fell over, and behind her came Granny Orla with a lantern, weeping and smiling at once. The old woman touched the worn map that peeped out of Ysra's pack and said that she had always known it was meant to be walked, and not kept in a box. Pell, who had been told a hundred times to be quiet, announced at the top of her small voice that she had saved a cupful of water for Ysra since the day she left.

Five days later the whole city crowded into the square before the Well-House, because the Rope Keeper had sent word that the Deep Well was rising. From the attic window of Maro's bakery, where they had spent the days in hiding, Ysra watched the old man lower his rope into the dark, count to a hundred aloud and haul it up again, hand over hand. The wet part was a full hand longer than the month before, and a roar of joy went up from ten thousand throats that she felt through the floorboards.

Then Rhodric Stane climbed the platform in a fresh blue robe, as clean and calm as though he had never raised his voice in his life, and lifted both arms for silence. It was the Guild, he cried, in a ringing voice, and his own brave engineers who had ridden into the Glass Desert, found the lost gate of the Channelwrights and opened the Silver Vein to save Oshenar. The crowd, which badly wanted to believe somebody, roared its gratitude, and Stane bowed low, with his hand on his heart.

In the middle of the cheering Ysra felt her father's hand tighten on hers, and she knew, with a certainty that surprised her, that she could not stay silent. She pulled back her hood, pushed through the crowd to the foot of the platform with the tally book under her arm, and said, in a voice that carried across the whole astonished square, “That is not true.” The cheering died away in widening circles, like a pond after a stone, until the only sound was the soft, steady rushing of the river.

Stane smiled sadly, the smile of a kindly uncle, and told the crowd that this poor child had suffered a terrible shock out in the desert and that her grief had confused her mind. At his nod two guards in blue coats stepped down from the platform and began to push their way through the crowd towards Ysra, and people drew back from her, uncertain, with murmurs rising like bees in a hive. For a moment she felt very small and very alone, and then a hand took hers on one side and another on the other.

Dorin Vell, thin and grey but upright, took his place on her left, and Teyo, grinning and dusty, on her right, and from the crowd behind them stepped Tobin the winch-man, holding up a great steel padlock. He told the hushed square that he had guarded the Stone Gate for months, with six of his friends, and that this lock with its silver seal was the lock that had held the river back. Every person who could read a seal could read this one, and a silence fell that was heavier than any shout.

Ysra opened Captain Harl's tally book and began to read out its figures in her clear, unhurried counting voice, barrel by barrel and week by week, the record of the water that had been taken. She laid them beside the fall of the rope, which every person in the square had watched with fear for months, and the two columns matched like the two halves of a torn page. Every page, she added, bore the signature of the captain of the Guild's own guard, who had kept it honestly and had sent it freely.

Stane's smile cracked at last, and he shouted that the book was forged, the lock a clumsy trick and these people rebels, bought and paid for by his enemies, who wished to rob the city of its great day. He was red in the face now, and his silver rings flashed as he flung his arms about, and the more he shouted the more the crowd began to hear what lay beneath his voice. Nobody was cheering any longer, and a great many people were looking, with slow and troubled eyes, from the Guildmaster to the girl with the book.

Elder Maris Thorne, the oldest member of the Well-Council, rose slowly from her stool at the side of the platform, leaning on a stick as old and dark as herself. She had not spoken in public for eleven years, and her thin dry voice was so quiet that the whole square leaned forward to hear it, which was exactly her intention. The Council, she said, would hear every side of this matter calmly in the great hall, and no person present, whatever his rank, would be arrested until it had done so.

For two days the Council sat in the great hall and listened, while the whole city waited in the street outside, to Tobin and his friends, to Dorin, to Teyo and above all to Ysra. They studied the padlock and the tally book, and walked along the long table where she had laid out her careful copies of the Channelwrights' paintings and tables, and they asked many hard questions. To every one of them she gave an exact answer, and not once in the two days did she raise her voice.

When the last witness had spoken, every member of the Well-Council raised a hand to strip Rhodric Stane of the Guildmaster's silver seal and to judge him in open court for theft and the unlawful imprisonment of Dorin Vell. The old Elder picked up the unsigned Law of Scarcity from the table, tore it in two with her thin hands and let the pieces fall. Stane, for the first time in his long and slippery life, found that he had nothing smooth left to say.

The Council's own guards, not the Guild's, led Stane out into the street, where the crowd fell silent as he passed, and then, slowly, as if the people were remembering how, began to cheer. At the back a thin man in a grey coat tried to slip out by a side door, but found his way blocked by Maro the baker and his two enormous sons. Fennick Dray's cold smile, which had once seemed so clever to him, vanished entirely as the baker's hand closed on his collar.

That night, in the quiet of the empty hall, Elder Maris asked Ysra, as one adult asks another, what the city ought to do now that Stane's rule had been broken. Ysra thought of the line that the Channelwrights had left in the painted tunnel, what the river gives, give on, and of the brass cup in her pocket, which had never once cheated anybody. Then she took a deep breath and, for the first time in her life, began to speak to the great and the wise as if she were one of them.

Ysra proposed what she called the Open Well Law, and she counted its three rules off on her fingers, one by one, in a voice that grew steadier with every word. The well, she said, would be measured in public every morning, so that no one could lie about what it held, and every household, rich or poor, would draw the same fair share by the same honest cup. The Stone Gate would be guarded by the city and the Sandwrights together, so that no single hand could ever close it again, since the river belonged to whoever was thirsty.

At sunrise, after a night of fierce and honest argument, the Council voted by eleven votes to one to pass the Open Well Law, and Elder Maris read it aloud from the same platform where Stane had stood. The single dissenting member, who feared that nothing so fair could possibly last, was quietly forgiven by everyone and bought a cup of tea by the baker. A great cheer rose from the square, and for a few moments it seemed that the whole city was laughing and crying at once.

The Council asked that the Vell family's brass cup, which had never cheated anyone in three generations, become the official measure of the city, and Dorin, smiling, took it from his daughter's hand and carried it into the square. There it was set into a niche on top of a pillar of white stone, with a small iron rail round it, where every person in Oshenar could see it and every merchant's cup could be checked against it. Ysra, watching from the crowd, found that she did not mind giving it away, since the smiths would cast her a twin by the end of the week and it had never really been hers alone.

On the first morning of the Open Well Law the queue stretched from the Well-House door across the square, and it was the quietest, most patient queue in the city's history, because everyone knew there would be enough. Little Pell stood first in the line, on tiptoe, holding up her chipped cup, and the Rope Keeper filled it to the brim by the measure of the brass cup while the whole square held its breath. She drank it down in one long gulp, announced that it tasted like the first water in the world, and politely asked whether she could have it all again tomorrow.

In the shade of the market awnings Ysra held out the finest dew-sail from her father's chest, the payment she had promised when they met, and Teyo took it as gently as if it were a sleeping bird. For once he did not say a word, but his eyes said a great deal, and he held the grey cloth against his cheek for a moment exactly as she had done. Then the Council's herald arrived with an invitation, which he read out in front of everyone: the Sandwrights were asked to be the keepers of the desert and of the Stone Gate, for as long as the river ran.

Teyo accepted for his people, with a formal bow, and Amma Zeri, standing at the back of the crowd, gave a small nod that said the whole of the Sandwrights agreed with him. For himself, he said with a grin, he would go on being what he had always been, a walker and a wind-reader, because a person who stood still might as well be a statue. But he promised that he would come back with the first wind of every spring, and that he would whistle at the gate so that Ysra would know.

As the weeks went by Dorin grew strong again, and one morning, sitting beside the window with a bowl of tea, he offered the shop to Ysra and said that it was hers now, every jar and every shelf. Ysra, who had been counting coins on the quilt, looked up and said that she would be a merchant, as he had been, and a keeper of the Stone Gate besides, since the river needed somebody who could count. Dorin laughed so hard that he spilled his tea, and said that in that case he would have to learn to keep the ledgers himself.

Along the great stone channel the people of Oshenar planted palm trees and olive groves and long rows of vegetables, and the dry plain slowly became a green belt that grew wider with every season. Dew-sails of every colour were hung over the roofs of the city, copies of Dorin's grey masterpiece woven by the Sandwright women, and each morning the rooftops sparkled as though they had been scattered with diamonds. Granny Orla's tiny fountain at last ran freely again, and she sat beside it all day, no longer selling anything, handing a cup to everyone who passed.

A year later a terrible drought struck the whole country, so that the rains failed for months, the wells of the far towns shrank to puddles and the distant plains turned the colour of old bone. In the days of the Guild, Ysra knew, a season like that would have meant panic, hoarding and a few rich households swimming in water while the rest went thirsty. This time the Silver Vein ran steadily, the gates held, the rope was read aloud every morning in the square, and the Open Well Law shared out every drop, cup by honest cup.

Every morning Ysra went to the Well-House with the Rope Keeper, read the rope and chalked the number in large figures on a black board in the square, so that nobody ever had to wonder what the well held. Little Pell, who was eight now and had decided to be a merchant, stood beside her with her own chipped cup and counted along out loud, and the whole queue, quite without meaning to, counted with them. It was a small ceremony, and Ysra, who had once believed that numbers were the only things in the world that behaved themselves, thought that they had never behaved so well.

At dawn, once again, Ysra carried her clay jars up to the roof and set them in a row, while the city below her woke slowly in a haze of green leaves and morning smoke. At the centre of Oshenar the Deep Well shone clear and full, its rope marked in hands for everyone to read, and on the pillar beside it the old brass cup caught the first sun. From beyond the wall came a long, low whistle on the wind, and Ysra, smiling, slipped the twin of that cup into her pocket and went down the fourteen stairs to meet her friend.
